Find the interval of convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(x-2)^n}{n}$, checking both endpoints.
questions.answer: Ratio test gives radius $R=1$, centered at $x=2$: $1<x<3$ tentatively. At $x=3$: $\sum\frac{1}{n}$ diverges (harmonic). At $x=1$: $\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{n}$ converges (alternating). Interval of convergence: $[1,3)$.
questions.explanation: Ratio test gives radius $R=1$, centered at $x=2$: $1<x<3$ tentatively. At $x=3$: $\sum\frac{1}{n}$ diverges (harmonic). At $x=1$: $\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{n}$ converges (alternating). Interval of convergence: $[1,3)$.

questions.q: Level 3 · Advanced Find the full interval of convergence (including endpoint behavior) for the power series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(2x - 1)^n}{n^2 \cdot 4^n}$.
questions.answer: Apply the Ratio Test: $L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{(2x - 1)^{n+1}}{(n+1)^2 4^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{n^2 4^n}{(2x - 1)^n} \right| = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{|2x - 1|}{4} = \frac{|2x - 1|}{4}$ Require $x$: $2x - 1 = 4$, giving $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{4^n}{n^2 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}$, which converges by the $p$-series test ($p = 2 > 1$). Endpoint $x = -3/2$: $2x - 1 = -4$, giving $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-4)^n}{n^2 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}$, which converges absolutely (since $\sum 1/n^2$ converges). Therefore, the interval of convergence is $\left[ -\frac{3}{2}, \frac{5}{2} \right]$.
questions.explanation: Apply the Ratio Test: $L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{(2x - 1)^{n+1}}{(n+1)^2 4^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{n^2 4^n}{(2x - 1)^n} \right| = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{|2x - 1|}{4} = \frac{|2x - 1|}{4}$ Require $x$: $2x - 1 = 4$, giving $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{4^n}{n^2 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}$, which converges by the $p$-series test ($p = 2 > 1$). Endpoint $x = -3/2$: $2x - 1 = -4$, giving $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-4)^n}{n^2 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}$, which converges absolutely (since $\sum 1/n^2$ converges). Therefore, the interval of convergence is $\left[ -\frac{3}{2}, \frac{5}{2} \right]$.

questions.q: Using the binomial series for $(1 - x^2)^{-1/2}$, derive the Maclaurin series expansion for $f(x) = \arcsin x$ up to and including the $x^5$ term. State its radius of convergence.
questions.target: Using Taylor series to evaluate a limit
questions.answer: 1. Recall the general binomial expansion $(1 + u)^p = 1 + pu + \frac{p(p-1)}{2!}u^2 + \dots$. Here $u = -x^2$ and $p = -1/2$: $(1 - x^2)^{-1/2} = 1 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)(-x^2) + \frac{(-1/2)(-3/2)}{2}(-x^2)^2 + O(x^6) = 1 + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{3}{8}x^4 + O(x^6).$ 2. Since $\arcsin x = \int_0^x \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-t^2}}\,dt$, integrate term-by-term: $\arcsin x = \int_0^x \left( 1 + \frac{1}{2}t^2 + \frac{3}{8}t^4 + \dots \right) dt = x + \frac{1}{6}x^3 + \frac{3}{40}x^5 + \dots$ 3. The binomial series converges for $|-x^2| < 1 \Rightarrow |x| < 1$, so the radius of convergence is $R = 1$.
questions.explanation: 1. Recall the general binomial expansion $(1 + u)^p = 1 + pu + \frac{p(p-1)}{2!}u^2 + \dots$. Here $u = -x^2$ and $p = -1/2$: $(1 - x^2)^{-1/2} = 1 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)(-x^2) + \frac{(-1/2)(-3/2)}{2}(-x^2)^2 + O(x^6) = 1 + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{3}{8}x^4 + O(x^6).$ 2. Since $\arcsin x = \int_0^x \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-t^2}}\,dt$, integrate term-by-term: $\arcsin x = \int_0^x \left( 1 + \frac{1}{2}t^2 + \frac{3}{8}t^4 + \dots \right) dt = x + \frac{1}{6}x^3 + \frac{3}{40}x^5 + \dots$ 3. The binomial series converges for $|-x^2| < 1 \Rightarrow |x| < 1$, so the radius of convergence is $R = 1$.

questions.q: Level 1 · FoundationsFind the radius of convergence $R$ for the power series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty n! (2x - 1)^n$.
questions.answer: Apply the Ratio Test: $L = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left| \frac{(n+1)! (2x - 1)^{n+1}}{n! (2x - 1)^n} \right| = |2x - 1| \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} (n+1).$ For any $x eq \frac{1}{2}$, this limit is $\infty$. The series converges only at its center $x = \frac{1}{2}$. Thus, the radius of convergence is $\mathbf{R = 0}$.
questions.explanation: Apply the Ratio Test: $L = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left| \frac{(n+1)! (2x - 1)^{n+1}}{n! (2x - 1)^n} \right| = |2x - 1| \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} (n+1).$ For any $x eq \frac{1}{2}$, this limit is $\infty$. The series converges only at its center $x = \frac{1}{2}$. Thus, the radius of convergence is $\mathbf{R = 0}$.

questions.q: Level 1 · FoundationsExpress the infinite summation limit as a definite integral on the interval $[0, 1]$ and evaluate it: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i^3}{n^4}.$
questions.answer: Factor $\frac{1}{n} = \Delta x$: $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i^3}{n^4} = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^3 \cdot \frac{1}{n}.$ Here $x_i = \frac{i}{n} = 0 + i\Delta x$ with $\Delta x = \frac{1}{n}$, matching the right Riemann sum of $f(x) = x^3$ on $[0, 1]$: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^3 \frac{1}{n} = \int_0^1 x^3\,dx = \left[ \frac{x^4}{4} \right]_0^1 = \frac{1^4}{4} - 0 = \mathbf{\frac{1}{4}}.$
questions.explanation: Factor $\frac{1}{n} = \Delta x$: $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i^3}{n^4} = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^3 \cdot \frac{1}{n}.$ Here $x_i = \frac{i}{n} = 0 + i\Delta x$ with $\Delta x = \frac{1}{n}$, matching the right Riemann sum of $f(x) = x^3$ on $[0, 1]$: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^3 \frac{1}{n} = \int_0^1 x^3\,dx = \left[ \frac{x^4}{4} \right]_0^1 = \frac{1^4}{4} - 0 = \mathbf{\frac{1}{4}}.$
